# Best Salesforce Alternatives for Small Business (2026): 7 CRMs Compared

 October 15, 2026 February 10, 2026 by Software Verdicts Team 

Prices checked Oct 15, 2026 on each vendor's official pricing page (salesforce.com, hubspot.com, pipedrive.com, freshworks.com, zoho.com, monday.com, close.com, copper.com). Prices are per user (seat) per month, billed yearly, unless noted. Written by the Software Verdicts team; we compare published plans and have not tested these tools hands-on.

Table of Contents

## Decision Snapshot

| Category | Winner | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best Free CRM | HubSpot CRM | Free plan with no time limit (2 users, 1,000 contacts) with pipelines and deal tracking |
| Best Visual Pipeline | Pipedrive | Pipeline-first design, fast onboarding, activity-based selling |
| Best Built-in Comms | Freshsales | Native phone, email, and chat at $9/user/mo |
| Best Customization | Zoho CRM | Salesforce-level flexibility at SMB pricing, 45+ Zoho app ecosystem |
| Best for Inside Sales | Close | Native Power Dialer + Predictive Dialer, SMS, email sequences |
| Best for Google Teams | Copper | Lives inside Gmail sidebar, automatic data capture from email |
| Best CRM + Project Mgmt | Monday Sales CRM | Visual board-based interface, connects CRM with operations |

HubSpot CRM is a safe starting point for one or two people with its free plan (2 users, 1,000 contacts); Zoho CRM's free plan allows 3 users. For sales-focused teams, Pipedrive delivers the cleanest pipeline experience while Close is purpose-built for phone-heavy outreach. Zoho CRM offers the deepest customization for teams that want Salesforce-like flexibility without the price or complexity.

## Pricing at a Glance (2026)

| CRM | Free Tier | Starting Paid Price | Top Tier Price |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salesforce (reference) | Yes (Free Suite) | $25/user/mo (Starter Suite) | $550/user/mo (Max) |
| HubSpot CRM | Yes (2 users, 1,000 contacts) | $20/seat/mo | From $150/seat/mo |
| Pipedrive | No | $14/user/mo | $79/user/mo |
| Freshsales | No (21-day trial) | $9/user/mo | $59/user/mo |
| Zoho CRM | Yes (3 users) | $14/user/mo | $40/user/mo (Enterprise) |
| Monday Sales CRM | No | $12/seat/mo | Custom |
| Close | No | $9/user/mo (Solo, 1 user) | $139/user/mo |
| Copper | No | $23/seat/mo | $99/seat/mo |

Pricing changes frequently. Always verify current rates on the vendor’s website.

Salesforce pricing HubSpot pricing Pipedrive pricing Freshsales pricing Zoho CRM pricing monday CRM pricing Close pricing Copper pricing

Yearly billing, prices checked Oct 15, 2026. Subject to change.

## Feature Comparison Matrix

| Feature | HubSpot | Pipedrive | Freshsales | Zoho CRM | Monday | Close | Copper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Free Tier | Yes (2 users) | No | No | Yes (3 users) | No | No | No |
| Built-in Calling | Add-on | Add-on | Yes (native) | Via Zoho Voice | No | Yes (Power/Predictive) | No |
| Native SMS | No | No | Yes | No | No | Yes | No |
| Email Sequences | Professional+ | Growth+ | Pro+ | Professional+ | Pro | Growth+ | Business |
| AI Features | Yes (higher tiers) | Yes (higher tiers) | Yes (Freddy AI) | Yes (Zia AI) | Limited | Limited | Limited |
| Visual Pipeline | Yes | Yes (core focus) | Yes | Yes | Yes (board-based) | Yes | Yes |
| Custom Workflows | Yes | Growth+ | Growth+ | Standard+ | Yes (no-code) | Yes | Professional+ |
| Google Workspace Native | No | No | No | No | No | No | Yes (core) |
| Marketing + Sales Combined | Yes | No | Limited | Yes (Zoho suite) | Yes (Work OS) | No | No |
| Project Management | No | No | No | Via Zoho Projects | Yes (core) | No | Professional+ |
| Auto Data Capture | Limited | Limited | Limited | Limited | No | Limited | Yes (Gmail) |
| Integration Count | 2,000+ | 500+ | 500+ | 900+ | 200+ | 100+ | 150+ |

## Who Should Choose What

Want to start free and scale later:

- HubSpot CRM — Free plan for 2 users and 1,000 contacts; Marketing, Sales, Service Hubs for growth
- Zoho CRM — Free plan for up to 3 users

Sales-driven team wanting pipeline focus:

- Pipedrive — Visual, drag-and-drop pipeline; activity-based selling; fast onboarding in 1–2 days

High-volume phone and email outreach:

- Close — Native Power Dialer, Predictive Dialer, SMS, and email sequences for inside sales teams
- Freshsales — Built-in phone, email, and chat at every tier ($9/user/mo entry)

Need Salesforce-like customization at SMB pricing:

- Zoho CRM — Custom modules, layouts, validation rules, Zia AI; 45+ integrated Zoho apps

Team runs on Google Workspace:

- Copper — Gmail sidebar integration, automatic data capture, Google Calendar and Drive sync

Want CRM + project management in one tool:

- Monday Sales CRM — Board-based visual interface; connects sales with operations and project tracking

Want a single platform for marketing + sales:

- HubSpot CRM — Marketing Hub + Sales Hub + Service Hub under one roof with 2,000+ marketplace apps

Salesforce dominates the CRM market. It powers enterprises across every industry, offers deep customization, and maintains one of the largest software ecosystems in the world. None of that is in dispute.

What is increasingly clear, however, is that Salesforce was not built with small businesses in mind — and the gap between what SMBs need and what Salesforce delivers continues to widen. For teams of five, ten, or even fifty people, simpler and more affordable CRM platforms now cover the same core workflows at a fraction of the cost and complexity.

This guide compares seven Salesforce alternatives purpose-built (or well-suited) for small businesses, covering features, pricing, strengths, and ideal use cases.

## Why Small Businesses Look for Salesforce Alternatives

Salesforce has a Free Suite and a Starter Suite at $25 per user per month — reasonable on paper. But teams that need more automation move to Pro Suite ($100/user/mo, billed yearly) or the Sales Cloud editions (Core $195, Advanced $395, Max $550 per user a month, billed yearly), where costs escalate rapidly. A ten-person sales team on Pro Suite runs $12,000 per year before add-ons, integrations, or consulting fees.

Beyond pricing, the most common reasons small businesses move away from Salesforce include:

- Complexity: Salesforce is built to serve organizations with dedicated administrators. Small teams without a Salesforce-certified admin often use only a fraction of available features while wrestling with configuration overhead.
- Implementation time: Full Salesforce deployments can take weeks or months. Many SMBs need a CRM they can set up and start using within days.
- Admin dependency: Customizing workflows, reports, and automations in Salesforce frequently requires specialized knowledge, creating bottlenecks for lean teams.
- Feature overload: For businesses that primarily need contact management, pipeline tracking, and basic automation, Salesforce's breadth becomes noise rather than value.

The alternatives below address these pain points in different ways — some through radical simplicity, others through competitive pricing, and several through both.

## 1. HubSpot CRM

### Overview

HubSpot occupies a unique position in the CRM market: it offers a free plan with no time limit (2 users, 1,000 contacts), so a very small business can start managing contacts and deals without spending anything. The free CRM includes contact management, deal pipelines, email tracking, meeting scheduling, and basic reporting.

For teams that need more — sales automation, sequences, custom reporting, and predictive lead scoring — HubSpot's Sales Hub starts at $20 per seat per month on the Starter plan, scaling through Professional (from $100/seat/mo) and Enterprise (from $150/seat/mo) tiers.

- Free tier with real functionality: Unlike most "free" CRMs that serve as glorified trials, HubSpot's free plan is usable long-term for very small teams.
- All-in-one platform: Marketing, sales, service, and operations tools live under one roof, eliminating the need to stitch together multiple SaaS products.
- Ease of use: HubSpot consistently ranks among the easiest CRMs to learn, with an intuitive interface and extensive free training through HubSpot Academy.
- Ecosystem: More than 2,000 apps in the HubSpot App Marketplace.

| Plan | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Free CRM | $0 (2 users, 1,000 contacts) |
| Sales Hub Starter | $20/seat/mo |
| Sales Hub Professional | From $100/seat/mo |
| Sales Hub Enterprise | From $150/seat/mo |

### Best Use Case

Small businesses that want a single platform for marketing and sales, especially those starting with zero budget and planning to scale into paid features over time.

## 2. Pipedrive

Pipedrive was built by salespeople for salespeople, and it shows. The entire platform revolves around a visual pipeline interface that makes it immediately clear where every deal stands. There are no marketing modules, no service desks — just sales, distilled to its essentials.

Pipedrive offers four plans, Lite, Growth, Premium, and Ultimate, from $14 to $79 per seat a month billed yearly ($24 to $99 monthly); automations start on Growth. There is no free plan, only a 14-day trial.

- Visual pipeline management: The drag-and-drop Kanban-style pipeline is one of the most intuitive in the CRM space.
- Activity-based selling: Pipedrive emphasizes scheduling and completing sales activities (calls, emails, meetings) rather than just tracking deal values.
- Fast onboarding: Most teams are fully operational within a day or two.
- Sales automation: Even the mid-tier plans include workflow automation, reducing manual data entry.

| Plan | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Lite | $14/seat/mo ($24 monthly) |
| Growth | $39/seat/mo ($49 monthly) |
| Premium | $59/seat/mo ($79 monthly) |
| Ultimate | $79/seat/mo ($99 monthly) |

### Best Use Case

Sales-driven SMBs that want a focused, visual CRM without the distractions of marketing or service features. Particularly effective for teams that rely on outbound sales processes.

## 3. Freshsales

Freshsales, part of Freshworks' product suite, combines CRM functionality with built-in phone, email, and chat — eliminating the need for separate communication tools. The platform includes Freddy AI, which provides lead scoring, deal insights, and next-best-action recommendations.

Freshworks' pricing page shows no free plan, only a 21-day free trial; paid plans range from $9 to $59 per user per month billed yearly ($11 to $71 monthly).

- Built-in communication channels: Native phone, email, chat, and SMS reduce tool sprawl and keep all customer interactions in one place.
- AI-powered insights: Freddy AI scores leads, detects deal risks, and suggests actions — features that typically require enterprise-tier pricing elsewhere.
- Affordable entry point: The Growth plan at $9/user/mo includes the Kanban view, basic workflows, and built-in chat, email, and phone; contact scoring starts on Pro ($39).
- Clean interface: Freshsales avoids the cluttered feel common in feature-rich CRMs.

| Plan | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Free trial | 21 days (no free plan listed) |
| Growth | $9/user/mo |
| Pro | $39/user/mo |
| Enterprise | $59/user/mo |

### Best Use Case

SMBs that handle a high volume of inbound communication (calls, emails, chat) and want those channels natively integrated with their CRM rather than relying on third-party connectors.

## 4. Zoho CRM

Zoho CRM is the CRM component of a massive ecosystem — over 45 Zoho applications covering everything from accounting (Zoho Books) to project management (Zoho Projects) to email hosting (Zoho Mail). For businesses that adopt multiple Zoho products, the integration depth is unmatched at this price point.

The CRM itself is highly customizable, offering modules, layouts, validation rules, and workflow automation that approach Salesforce-level flexibility without the Salesforce-level complexity or cost.

- Deep customization: Custom modules, fields, layouts, and validation rules allow Zoho CRM to adapt to virtually any business process.
- Zoho ecosystem: Tight integration with 45+ Zoho apps creates an all-in-one business suite at SMB pricing.
- Zia AI assistant: Conversational AI for predictions, anomaly detection, and workflow suggestions (available on higher tiers).
- Competitive pricing: Enterprise-grade features at a fraction of Salesforce's cost.

| Plan | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Free | $0 (up to 3 users) |
| Standard | $14/user/mo |
| Professional | $23/user/mo |
| Enterprise | $40/user/mo |
| Ultimate | Price not listed on the US page |

### Best Use Case

Small businesses that need extensive customization or plan to use multiple business applications from a single vendor. Especially strong for companies that want Salesforce-like flexibility at a lower price and are willing to invest time in initial setup.

## 5. Monday Sales CRM

Monday Sales CRM extends Monday.com's popular Work OS into sales territory. It inherits the visual, board-based interface that made Monday.com a project management favorite and applies it to contact management, deal tracking, and sales automation.

The result is a CRM that feels less like traditional CRM software and more like a flexible workspace — familiar to anyone already using Monday.com for other business functions.

- Visual, board-based interface: Highly intuitive for teams that think visually. Boards, columns, and views are endlessly configurable.
- Work OS integration: Sales CRM connects directly with Monday.com's project management, marketing, and operations tools.
- No-code automations: Building automations requires no technical skills — "when X happens, do Y" logic is built with dropdowns and natural language.
- Collaboration-friendly: Built-in communication, file sharing, and activity tracking keep teams aligned.

| Plan | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Basic | $12/seat/mo ($18 monthly) |
| Standard | $17/seat/mo ($25 monthly) |
| Pro | $28/seat/mo ($41 monthly) |
| Ultimate (formerly Enterprise) | Custom pricing |

Prices billed yearly, checked Oct 15, 2026 on monday.com/crm/pricing. Seats are chosen with a team-size picker.

### Best Use Case

Teams already using Monday.com for project management or operations that want their CRM in the same environment. Also strong for visually oriented teams that find traditional CRM interfaces restrictive.

## 6. Close

Close is built for inside sales teams — the kind that sell primarily through phone calls, emails, and SMS rather than in-person meetings. Built-in calling, SMS, and email come on every plan; the power dialer and Workflows (sequences) start on Growth, and the predictive dialer is on Scale.

Calling features are included in the plans, which range from $9 (Solo, 1 user) to $139 per user per month billed yearly ($19 to $149 monthly); call and SMS usage is billed at cost.

- Built-in calling: Power dialer and predictive dialer are native features, not add-ons. Live call coaching is on the Scale plan.
- Native SMS: Send and receive text messages directly within the CRM.
- Email sequences: Automated multi-step email sequences with customizable triggers and timing.
- Speed-focused UI: The interface is optimized for high-volume outreach — minimizing clicks between calls and reducing data entry.

| Plan | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Solo (1 user) | $9/user/mo ($19 monthly) |
| Essentials | $35/user/mo ($49 monthly) |
| Growth | $99/user/mo ($109 monthly) |
| Scale | $139/user/mo ($149 monthly) |

### Best Use Case

Inside sales teams and SDR (Sales Development Representative) teams that rely heavily on cold calling, email outreach, and SMS. Close is purpose-built for high-volume, velocity-based sales motions.

## 7. Copper

Copper is a CRM designed to live entirely within Google Workspace. It integrates directly with Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Drive, and Google Contacts, pulling CRM functionality into the tools many small businesses already use daily.

Rather than asking users to learn a new interface, Copper surfaces contacts, deals, and activity tracking inside Gmail's sidebar — reducing context switching and accelerating adoption.

- Native Google Workspace integration: Copper pulls data directly from Gmail, Calendar, and Drive. Contacts and companies are created automatically from email interactions.
- Minimal learning curve: For teams already in Google Workspace, Copper feels like an extension of their existing workflow rather than a separate application.
- Automatic data capture: Emails, meetings, and files are logged to contact records without manual entry.
- Relationship tracking: Built-in tools for tracking interaction history, relationship health, and follow-up reminders.

| Plan | Cost |
| --- | --- |
| Basic | $23/seat/mo ($29 monthly) |
| Professional | $59/seat/mo ($69 monthly) |
| Business | $99/seat/mo ($134 monthly) |

### Best Use Case

Small businesses running on Google Workspace that want a CRM embedded in their existing email and calendar workflow. Particularly effective for relationship-driven businesses (consulting, agencies, professional services) where email is the primary communication channel.

## Comparison Table

| CRM | Starting Price | Free Plan | Built-in Calling | AI Features | Best For |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HubSpot | $20/seat/mo | Yes (2 users) | Add-on | Yes (higher tiers) | All-in-one marketing + sales |
| Pipedrive | $14/user/mo | No | Add-on | Yes (higher tiers) | Visual pipeline management |
| Freshsales | $9/user/mo | No (21-day trial) | Yes (native) | Yes (Freddy AI) | Communication-heavy sales |
| Zoho CRM | $14/user/mo | Yes (3 users) | Yes (via Zoho) | Yes (Zia AI) | Customization + ecosystem |
| Monday Sales CRM | $12/user/mo | No | No | Limited | Visual teams / Monday.com users |
| Close | $9/user/mo (Solo) | No | Yes (native dialer) | Limited | Inside sales / cold outreach |
| Copper | $23/seat/mo | No | No | Limited | Google Workspace teams |

## Summary

Each of these seven platforms addresses a specific pain point that drives small businesses away from Salesforce. HubSpot offers a free plan with no time limit and the broadest feature set. Pipedrive delivers focused simplicity for pipeline-driven teams. Freshsales bundles communication tools that would otherwise require separate subscriptions. Zoho CRM provides Salesforce-level customization at SMB pricing. Monday Sales CRM turns CRM into a visual, collaborative workspace. Close arms inside sales teams with native calling and SMS. Copper embeds CRM directly into Google Workspace.

The common thread: all seven are faster to implement, simpler to manage, and less expensive to operate than Salesforce for small business use cases. The differences lie in where each platform focuses its strengths — and matching that focus to how a particular business actually sells is what separates a CRM that gets used from one that collects dust.

Prices checked Oct 15, 2026 and subject to change. Visit each provider's website for the most up-to-date information.

Best CRM for small teams in 2026: 6 tools ranked — BizTooling

# Best CRM for small teams in 2026: 6 tools ranked 

 Six CRMs ranked for teams under ten people, on what a founder can set up alone this week and what still runs without a dedicated admin. 

 Ada Reyes 

 Updated August 2026 9 min read 

A small team buying a CRM is not making a scaled-down version of the enterprise decision. There is no admin who owns the object model, no revenue operations hire who reads the release notes, and no budget for an implementation partner. Whoever sets it up on Monday is also the person explaining it to the second hire on Friday, and if the tool needs a manual to get past the first pipeline, most teams under ten people just stop using it and drift back to a spreadsheet.

That changes which features matter. Depth a solo admin would configure over months is a liability rather than a selling point when there is no solo admin. This ranks six CRMs on what a founder or a first ops hire can get running alone this week, and what still holds up once a third or fourth person joins.

## Summary

1. Pipedrive: best for the simplest pipeline running today, with almost no setup thinking required.
2. Attio: best for a team that expects to outgrow a bare pipeline within the year.
3. Folk: best for a founder still selling from a contact list and LinkedIn, before there is a formal pipeline.
4. HubSpot: best for a team that also needs marketing tools on the same free login.
5. Zoho CRM: best when a tight budget still needs invoicing and support bundled in.
6. monday CRM: best for a team already living on monday boards for delivery work.

## What decides it at this size

Team size changes the math on three things a generic buying guide tends to skip.

- Time to first value. How long from signup to a rep working in it, with nobody free to spend a week on configuration.
- Cost at two, three, or five seats. The sticker price at fifty seats says nothing about what a five-person team pays, and seat minimums or onboarding fees land hardest on the smallest accounts.
- Room to grow. A data model that fits fine at five people can force a switch at fifteen, and a switch a year in costs more than the setup did.

The full picture on setup cost and what breaks later, across a wider set of platforms, is in the breakdown of the best CRM tools by year-two cost. A team whose sales motion is likely to change shape faster than its headcount, such as one that just closed a funding round, weighs some of these tradeoffs differently, covered separately in the ranking built for startups.

## Where small teams get burned

Three patterns account for most of the wasted subscriptions we hear about.

The first is the blank canvas. A platform built for a configurable enterprise process hands a five-person team the same empty object model a two-hundred-person revenue operations function gets, and nobody on a small team has the time to decide what a “deal” should contain before they can start using it.

The second is the seat minimum. Three-seat floors and per-user onboarding fees are rounding errors at fifty seats and a real percentage of the bill at three.

The third is picking for a future team that has not been hired yet. A founder buys the platform built for a twenty-person sales org because it looks more serious, then spends the first year fighting fields and permissions nobody needs yet.

## The six best CRMs for small teams in 2026

Figures below are quoted per seat, per month, on an annual plan, unless stated otherwise.

### 1. Pipedrive

Best for: a small team that needs a shared pipeline live before the end of the day.

Pipedrive takes the top spot because there is nothing to learn before using it. A board of deal cards moving through stages is a concept everyone already understands, so a founder can hand it to a new hire without a training call. Nothing here is unique, and that is the point: the whole product is the pipeline, with none of the surrounding modules a small team has to ignore to get value.

First week:

- A rep can drag a deal to a new stage on day one, no walkthrough needed.
- Spreadsheet imports map cleanly onto contacts, organizations, and deals.
- Two-way email sync starts logging activity against the right deal immediately.

Where it strains:

- There is no free plan, so three people on Lite run to roughly $500 a year before anything else is added.
- Automation waits until Growth, so the entry tier is a manual pipeline.
- Nothing beyond contacts, organizations, and deals, so a support or delivery workflow needs a separate tool.

Pricing: entry-level Lite runs $14, then $39 on Growth, $59 on Premium, and $79 on the top Ultimate tier.

### 2. Attio

Best for: a small team that expects to outgrow a bare pipeline within the year.

Attio costs the small team a little more setup thought than a pure pipeline tool, since it asks what objects the business runs on rather than assuming contacts and deals are enough. That five minutes of thinking pays off the day the team adds a second product line or a partner motion, because the change is a new object rather than a new tool. Connecting an inbox and calendar builds out contact and company history in the background, so the record is not empty even before the team has typed anything, and the free tier covers three seats with no time limit.

First week:

- Free for up to three seats, with no seat minimum to clear first.
- Objects, attributes, and views are configured in the interface, with no certification needed.
- Email and calendar sync fills company and contact history from day one.

Where it strains:

- Defining objects up front is a real decision, however brief, versus a pipeline tool that needs none.
- Call intelligence and sequences sit on the Pro plan and above.
- The flexibility that pays off later is more configuration than the smallest teams strictly need on day one.

Pricing: the free plan covers three seats, Plus is $35, Pro is $79 and adds call intelligence, and Enterprise is custom.

### 3. Folk

Best for: a founder still working a contact list and LinkedIn.

Folk fits a stage before a real sales process exists. A browser extension pulls contacts straight from LinkedIn searches, light pipelines organize them by stage, and the entire setup runs in about an hour with nothing to configure first. It is deliberately narrow, and for a founder working their own network, that narrowness is the appeal rather than a limitation.

First week:

- The folkX extension captures contacts and companies from LinkedIn in one click.
- Auto-merge and deduplication clean up the list on import.
- No object modeling, since the data model is intentionally just people, companies, and deals.

Where it strains:

- Per-member pricing starts higher than several tools here that cover far more ground.
- Automation and reporting stay thin once a second rep who did not build the list joins.
- The API needed for real integrations only opens up from the Premium plan.

Pricing: billed per member, $24 on Standard, $48 on Premium, and Enterprise pricing beginning around $80.

### 4. HubSpot

Best for: a team that needs marketing and sales on the same free login.

HubSpot works for a small team that has not split marketing and sales into separate jobs yet. Forms, a shared inbox, and basic email tracking sit next to the pipeline in the same free account, so the same login covers both jobs instead of stitching two products together. The trap is timing: the jump to Starter and then Professional brings a real price step, and a one-time $1,500 onboarding fee lands right when the team can least absorb a surprise cost.

First week:

- Two people can run a shared inbox, forms, and a pipeline without paying anything.
- Guided setup and templates get a non-technical founder to a working CRM fast.
- Marketing sends and sales follow-ups draw on the same contact record from day one.

Where it strains:

- Object customization is limited on the free and Starter tiers.
- The move to Professional brings both a bigger bill and a $1,500 onboarding fee.
- Deeper automation and reporting stay locked until that tier.

Pricing: free for two seats, $7 on Starter, a sharp step to $90 on Professional, then Enterprise from $150.

### 5. Zoho CRM

Best for: a tight budget that still needs invoicing and support bundled in.

A founding team on a strict budget gets more configuration per dollar out of Zoho than anything else on this list, and the same login can eventually cover invoicing and support through the wider Zoho suite. Three users can run on the no-cost edition indefinitely, which suits a founding team exactly. The tradeoff is coherence: connecting Zoho CRM to Zoho Books or Zoho Desk is real setup work that a solo founder has to schedule for themselves.

First week:

- Three users can start on the no-cost edition with no trial clock running.
- Custom fields and page layouts are available from the first login.
- Web form capture and lead assignment need some initial setup to work well.

Where it strains:

- Wiring Zoho’s separate applications together takes real integration time, not a toggle.
- Validation rules and deeper process controls wait until Professional and above.
- Reporting stays shallower than tools designed around one unified record.

Pricing: free for three users, then $14 (Standard), $23 (Professional), $40 (Enterprise), and $52 (Ultimate).

### 6. monday CRM

Best for: a team already living on monday boards for delivery.

If the team already runs projects on monday, adding the CRM keeps sales and delivery on one Work OS instead of two systems that need syncing. Board setup is quick for anyone who already knows the interface. The catch for a small team specifically: every plan requires at least three seats and there is no free option, so even the smallest possible account costs more than it would elsewhere before a single add-on.

First week:

- A team that already runs projects on monday recognizes the boards immediately.
- Ready-made automation recipes cover lead intake and follow-ups without custom setup.
- WorkForms let the team start collecting leads without wiring a separate tool.

Where it strains:

- Buying for two people still means paying for three seats, since there is no way around the floor.
- Email sync and most native integrations only unlock from the Standard plan.
- Capture is manual by default, since monday was built for work tracking rather than customer records.

Pricing: every tier requires three seats minimum, with Basic at $12, Standard at $17, Pro at $28, and Enterprise custom.

## FAQs

### Should a small team pay for a CRM before hiring a salesperson?

Only once deals are being lost track of, not before. A founder closing the first handful of customers from a spreadsheet or inbox is usually fine there. The switch is worth making when a lead goes cold because nobody remembers to follow up, or when two people can no longer tell from memory who owns which conversation.

### How many seats should a small team buy at first?

Buy for the people using it now, not the hires planned for next quarter. Seat minimums and annual commitments make it expensive to guess high, and every platform on this list makes adding a seat later a two-minute action rather than a renegotiation.

Choosing a CRM for a Twenty-Person Company - Global Brands Drive

# Choosing a CRM for a Twenty-Person Company

Eight CRMs priced at eight seats from their own published pages — and why the tier you pick moves the bill more than the brand does.

By Global Brands Drive Editorial Team September 6, 2026 15 min read

Eight vendors priced at eight seats, from their own published pages.

 In this article 

At eight CRM seats and annual billing, the tier a twenty-person company actually needs costs between US$2,688 and US$10,140 in year one across eight vendors whose prices are published. That is a 3.8× spread for what is broadly the same job. But the vendor is not the decision that moves the bill most. Moving up one tier — usually because you want workflow automation — costs 1.69× more per seat at one vendor and 12.86× more at another. Pick the tier before you pick the brand.

Every figure below is a list price read from the vendor’s own public pricing page on 5 September 2026, at annual billing, and re-read the same day. Two vendors could not be priced at all; they are named, and why, further down.

US$2,688 Lowest year-one cost, 8 seats, mid tier monday CRM Pro, list price

US$10,140 Highest year-one cost, same configuration HubSpot Sales Hub Professional, including onboarding

7.6× Difference between vendors in what moving up one tier costs per seat

25.8% Share of year one taken by one fixed onboarding fee at four seats

## The scenario, stated before the numbers

“A CRM for a twenty-person company” is not a price until you say how many people will hold a licence. Almost all of this market is priced per seat, so seat count is an input, not a detail.

The scenario used throughout is eight seats — six people selling, two managing or running operations, inside a company of twenty. Everything is tested again at four and sixteen seats further down, because that assumption does more work than any other in the model.

Two tiers are priced for each vendor: the cheapest paid plan that a team can actually share, and the tier above it. The step between them is where the interesting numbers are, because that step is what a company buys when it stops wanting a shared contact list and starts wanting the software to do something on its own.

## The step up a tier is the decision, and it is not priced consistently

Every vendor here sells a cheap plan and a more capable one. What differs enormously is the size of the step between them.

What moving up one tier costs

Mid-tier price divided by entry-tier price, per seat, annual billing

 

Source: Calculated by Global Brands Drive from the list prices in the table above, each read from the vendor’s own pricing page on 5 September 2026. Chart by Global Brands Drive.

Insightly’s step is 1.69×. HubSpot Sales Hub’s is 12.86×. The gap between those two multiples is 7.6× — larger than the gap between the highest and lowest year-one totals at a fixed tier.

This is not a flaw in anyone’s pricing. A gently rising ladder and a steep one are both ordinary commercial designs, and they suit different buyers: a shallow step lets a small team upgrade without a budget conversation, while a steep step usually accompanies a much larger jump in what the tier contains. HubSpot’s Starter, at US$7 a seat a month on annual billing, is among the cheapest paid entry points in this group; the distance to Professional is large partly because Starter is priced so low.

The question is not “which CRM is cheapest”. It is “which tier do we actually need” — and only then, “who prices that tier well”.

The practical consequence: a shortlist built at the entry tier can invert completely once the team decides it needs the tier above. If there is any chance of that within a year, price both tiers for every vendor before choosing, not after.

## Seat count moves the bill as much as vendor choice does

It is tempting to treat seat count as an afterthought and the vendor as the real decision. In this data they are worth about the same.

So a quote that does not state both the tier and the seat count is not a price. Note also the seat rules that bite at the edges: Attio’s Plus plan is published as “Up to 10” seats, so a sixteen-seat team on that plan moves to Pro; monday CRM publishes that “Plans start from 3 users”, which sets a floor under the smallest teams.

## A fixed fee falls hardest on the smallest team

One vendor in this group publishes a required one-time onboarding fee alongside its mid tier. Because that fee is fixed rather than per seat, its weight depends entirely on how many seats it is spread across.

Two things follow. First, the annual commitment is worth very different amounts depending on the plan — from nothing at all on Salesforce’s Starter Suite, which its page describes as “Billed monthly or annually” at the same figure, to a large difference on HubSpot’s Sales Hub Starter. Second, some tiers do not offer the choice: Salesforce publishes Pro Suite and everything above it as “(Billed annually)”, and Insightly’s page states “All prices USD, billed annually”. Where there is no monthly option, the twelve-month commitment is part of the product, not a discount you elected to take.

## Two vendors we could not price, and what we did about it

Two well-known CRMs are absent from every figure above, and the reason is the same in both cases: we could not read a price for them in US dollars on the pages we checked, and this publication does not estimate.

- Zoho CRM. On the pricing and comparison pages we checked, every figure rendered in Indian rupees, including on the US-English URL, and the currency selector did not change the rendered numbers for us. The published rupee prices are clear and internally consistent; converting them ourselves would have produced a US dollar figure Zoho does not publish, so we left them out. Zoho does publish a free tier described as “Forever free, for 3 users”, and its pages note that “Local taxes (VAT, GST, etc.) will be charged in addition to the prices mentioned.”
- Capsule CRM. The paid-tier prices are loaded into the page after it renders and did not appear in the text we could read. What did appear is the billing basis — “Per user, per month. Billed Annually” — and the free tier’s limits of two users and 250 contacts. Both vendors may well publish or quote these figures elsewhere; we did not have them, so we did not estimate them.

The same rule removed three other figures: month-to-month rates for Pipedrive and Freshsales, whose pages showed a billing toggle but rendered only the annual view for us, and Salesforce’s highest tier, which prints a list rate and simultaneously directs the buyer to contact the company.

## What to do on Monday

1. Fix the seat count first, in writing Decide who actually needs a licence, and add the growth you expect within twelve months. Every price on this page is per seat, so this number sets the bill more than the logo on the invoice does.
2. Decide which tier you need before you shortlist Write down the one capability that would make you leave the entry tier — usually automation of a step someone currently does by hand. If you cannot name it, you are buying the entry tier.
3. Price both tiers at every vendor on the shortlist The ranking at the entry tier is not the ranking at the tier above it. On this data the step varies by 7.6× between vendors, so a shortlist built at one tier can be wrong at the other.
4. Add the one-time fees and the seat rules before you compare A required onboarding charge, a minimum seat count and a maximum seat count are all published, and all change the answer. None of them appear in a headline per-seat price.

And the case for doing nothing yet. If nobody can name the manual step the software is supposed to remove, the honest answer is that this is not yet a purchase. Several vendors here publish a free tier — HubSpot for two users, Attio for three, Zoho for three, Capsule for two — and every one of them caps at two or three seats, which makes them a way to test the shape of the thing rather than a way to run a twenty-person company. Use one for a month, find the step that hurts, then come back to this table knowing what you are buying.

## How every number here was calculated

Every figure is arithmetic on published list prices, and you should be able to reproduce all of it. The convention throughout: annual billing wherever a vendor offers the choice, prices as printed on the vendor’s own page, and no conversion between currencies.

Year one at eight seats, mid tier

Every cell carries its unit. Prices read 5 September 2026.

| Vendor and plan | Working | Year one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| monday CRM Pro | US$28/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 | US$2,688 |
| Freshsales Pro | US$39/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 | US$3,744 |
| Insightly Professional | US$49/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 | US$4,704 |
| Pipedrive Premium | US$59/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 | US$5,664 |
| Attio Pro | US$79/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 | US$7,584 |
| Close Growth | US$99/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 | US$9,504 |
| Salesforce Pro Suite | US$100/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 | US$9,600 |
| HubSpot Sales Hub Professional | US$90/seat/mo × 8 seats × 12 + US$1,500 onboarding | US$10,140 |
| Range | US$10,140 ÷ US$2,688 | 3.77× |

The tier-step multiple is the mid-tier per-seat price divided by the entry-tier per-seat price for the same vendor: for example US$90 ÷ US$7 = 12.86 for HubSpot Sales Hub, and US$49 ÷ US$29 = 1.69 for Insightly. The 7.6× headline is 12.86 ÷ 1.69. The onboarding shares are US$1,500 divided by the year-one total at each seat count.

Three assumptions are worth naming because they are choices rather than published figures. Eight seats is an assumption about how a twenty-person company staffs a CRM, not a survey finding. Which plan counts as “entry” and which as “mid” is our judgement about what a team of this size would actually consider, and a different reader could reasonably pair different tiers. And list price is not transaction price — none of these figures account for negotiation, promotions or non-profit and startup programmes, several of which the vendors mention on their own pages.

## Choosing a CRM: common questions

### How much should a twenty-person company spend on a CRM?

On published list prices at annual billing, eight seats on a mid-tier plan cost between US$2,688 and US$10,140 in year one across the eight vendors priced here. The entry tier for the same eight seats runs from US$672 to US$3,360. Which of those two ranges applies to you depends on whether you need the software to automate anything.

### Is a cheaper CRM a false economy?

Not necessarily, and the data does not answer it either way — these are prices, not quality judgements. What the data does show is that the gap between a vendor’s own two tiers is often larger than the gap between vendors, so “cheap” and “expensive” usually describe a tier choice rather than a brand.

### Does annual billing always save money?

No. Among the plans that publish both rates, the difference ranges from 0.0% on Salesforce’s Starter Suite, which its page prices identically either way, to 185.7% on HubSpot Sales Hub Starter. And some tiers publish no monthly option at all, in which case the annual commitment is a condition rather than a saving.

### What do the free CRM tiers actually give you?

Every free tier we found caps at two or three seats: HubSpot Sales Hub Free at two users, Attio Free at three, Zoho CRM at “Forever free, for 3 users”, Capsule at two users and 250 contacts. Several other vendors offer a time-limited trial rather than a free tier. None is a way to run a twenty-person sales team; all are a reasonable way to test one.

### What is not included in these prices?

One-time onboarding where a vendor requires it, telephony and call recording where they are sold separately, add-ons priced per user or per usage block, local taxes, and anything bought outside the plan. Only the HubSpot onboarding fee is included in the totals above, because it is the only required one-time fee published by the vendors priced here.

### Why are Zoho CRM and Capsule not in the comparison?

Because we could not read a US dollar price for them on the pages we checked — Zoho’s figures rendered in rupees for us, and Capsule’s paid-tier prices load into the page after it renders. Rather than convert or estimate, we left both out and said so. They may well publish those figures elsewhere.
